title: Saudi Arabia eVisa: The Complete Tourist Guide
excerpt: Who is eligible, how to apply in 10 minutes, costs, validity and the mistakes to avoid.
author: VisitSaudiArab Team
content:
Saudi Arabia's tourist eVisa has opened the Kingdom to leisure travellers from more than 60 countries. Applications are made online at the official portal, take about ten minutes, and approvals typically arrive within minutes to a couple of days.

The visa costs SAR 535 including mandatory medical insurance, is valid for one year, and allows multiple entries with stays of up to 90 days per visit. Holders of valid US, UK or Schengen visas, and residents of those countries, may be eligible for a visa on arrival.

Apply only through the official government portal — third-party sites charge large markups for the same visa. Print or save a copy of your eVisa to show at check-in and immigration. Passports must be valid for at least six months on arrival.

Note that the tourist eVisa does not permit Hajj; Umrah is permitted outside the Hajj season, but always check the current rules before booking religious travel.

title: Best Time to Visit Saudi Arabia (Month by Month)
excerpt: Desert winters, highland summers, festival seasons and Ramadan — when to go where.
author: VisitSaudiArab Team
content:
For most travellers, October to March is the golden window: Riyadh, Jeddah and AlUla enjoy warm days and cool evenings, the desert is comfortable for camping and hiking, and the big festivals — Riyadh Season, Winter at Tantora, the Grand Prix — all run in these months.

Summer flips the map. While the lowlands exceed 40°C, the Asir highlands around Abha and Taif stay green and mild, making June to September the perfect time for the mountains — and for Jeddah Season on the coast if you plan around the afternoon heat.

Ramadan shifts each year and brings a special atmosphere: days are quiet and many restaurants close until sunset, but evenings come alive with iftar feasts and late-night souqs. Tourist sites remain open, and hotel rates often drop.

title: Dress Code & Etiquette in Saudi Arabia
excerpt: What to wear, what has changed, and the courtesies that go a long way.
author: VisitSaudiArab Team
content:
Saudi Arabia has relaxed dramatically, but modest dress remains the norm in public. Women are no longer required to wear the abaya or headscarf — loose clothing covering shoulders and knees is appropriate everywhere except holy sites, where more conservative dress applies. Men should avoid shorts in formal settings; everywhere else, smart casual works.

A few courtesies matter: accept Arabic coffee and dates when offered, use your right hand for eating and greeting, and ask before photographing people — especially women. Public displays of affection are frowned upon.

During prayer times some shops close briefly; treat it as a chance to pause with a coffee rather than an inconvenience. Alcohol is prohibited nationwide — do not attempt to bring any into the country.

title: Getting Around Saudi Arabia: Trains, Flights & Road Trips
excerpt: Domestic flights, the Haramain and Riyadh–Dammam trains, driving rules and ride-hailing.
author: VisitSaudiArab Team
content:
Saudi Arabia is vast — flying is often the sensible choice. Saudia, Flynas and Flyadeal connect all major cities, and fares between Riyadh, Jeddah and Abha are frequently under SAR 300 one-way when booked ahead.

Two rail lines matter to visitors: the Haramain High-Speed Railway links Makkah, Jeddah and Madinah at 300 km/h, and the Riyadh–Dammam line crosses to the Gulf in about 4 hours. Riyadh's new metro has transformed getting around the capital.

Driving is on the right, roads are excellent, and visitors can drive on many foreign licences for up to a year. Rent a 4WD for desert destinations like the Edge of the World; in cities, Uber and Careem are cheap and everywhere. Distances are long — plan fuel stops on remote highways.

title: A First-Timer's Guide to Saudi Food
excerpt: Kabsa to mutabbaq, Arabic coffee etiquette, and where to find the real local kitchens.
author: VisitSaudiArab Team
content:
Start with kabsa — spiced rice with chicken, lamb or camel — the national dish, best eaten communal-style at a floor-seating restaurant. Then branch out: jareesh (cracked wheat with yoghurt), saleeg (Taif's creamy rice), and the Hijazi breakfast staples of foul and tamees bread straight from clay ovens.

Arabic coffee (qahwa) is a ritual, not just a drink: lightly roasted, cardamom-scented, poured in small cups, always with dates. Your cup will be refilled until you give it a gentle shake.

For street food, look for mutabbaq (stuffed pancakes) and sambosa, especially during Ramadan evenings. In Jeddah, eat seafood at the fish market restaurants where you pick your fish and they grill it on the spot. The modern dining scenes of Riyadh's Bujairi Terrace and Jeddah's waterfront now rival any Gulf city.

title: How Much Does a Saudi Arabia Trip Cost?
excerpt: Realistic daily budgets from backpacker to luxury, plus the money-saving tips locals use.
author: VisitSaudiArab Team
content:
Saudi Arabia suits most budgets. A comfortable mid-range trip runs SAR 600–1,000 (USD 160–265) per person per day: a 4-star hotel at SAR 350–500, restaurant meals at SAR 40–80, ride-hailing across town for SAR 15–30, and attraction tickets from free to SAR 100.

Budget travellers can manage on SAR 250–400 a day using 3-star hotels, local restaurants (a kabsa feast rarely tops SAR 30) and intercity buses. At the top end, AlUla's desert resorts and the Red Sea islands run into the thousands per night — worth it for a once-in-a-trip splurge.

Cards are accepted almost everywhere, including taxis and souqs; keep a little cash for small shops and tips. Tipping around 10% is customary in restaurants. Book festival-period hotels far ahead — prices spike hard during Riyadh Season and race weekends.
